posts.title: MCP at the edge changes the game for GTM pipelines
posts.hook: Cloudflare just shipped native MCP support in Workers. If you're building GTM infrastructure, this matters more than you think.
posts.body:
Cloudflare just shipped native MCP support in Workers. If you're building GTM infrastructure, this matters more than you think.

I run enrichment pipelines that hit 6+ APIs per prospect. Right now that's a Python script on a cron, running from my Mac Mini. It works. But latency compounds, cold starts bite, and scaling past a few hundred records per batch means babysitting.

MCP at the edge means your AI agents can call tools (enrichment APIs, CRM writes, scoring functions) from Cloudflare's network. Sub-50ms round trips. No server to manage.

The practical version of this for GTM engineers:

→ Enrichment that runs as prospects hit your forms, not in a nightly batch
→ Scoring that happens at ingest, not after the SDR already pinged the lead
→ Agent tools that live at the edge instead of behind your VPN

I'm porting one of my Deepline enrichment scripts to a Worker this week to see if the DX holds up. The promise is real. Whether it's production-ready for complex multi-step pipelines... that's what I want to test.

The direction is clear though. The GTM stack is moving from "run a script on a schedule" to "react in real time at the edge." And the teams that figure this out first get cleaner data, faster.

remixes.hook: I've been running GTM enrichment pipelines from a Mac Mini for two years. That setup just got an expiration date.
remixes.body:
I've been running GTM enrichment pipelines from a Mac Mini for two years. That setup just got an expiration date.

Cloudflare shipped native MCP support in Workers. For most people, that's a developer tools headline. For anyone running multi-API enrichment at scale, it's an architecture shift.

Here's my current flow: a Python script fires on cron, hits Apollo, Exa, Clearbit, and three other APIs per prospect. Sequential calls. Cold starts when the machine sleeps. Latency stacks. At 500 records per batch, I'm babysitting the process.

MCP at the edge rewrites this. Each tool call runs at the nearest Cloudflare node. The orchestration layer lives at the edge, not on my local machine. I can fan out enrichment calls in parallel across 300+ global locations instead of sequentially from one box.

The practical implications:

1. Enrichment latency drops from seconds per record to milliseconds.
2. No more cron babysitting. The pipeline is always warm.
3. Scaling from 500 to 50,000 records per batch becomes a config change, not an infrastructure project.
4. The MCP protocol means I define tools once and they're callable from any agent framework.

I'm not migrating tomorrow. But I'm prototyping a Workers-based enrichment layer this week. The economics alone justify the experiment.

Most GTM engineers focus on the per-call pricing of enrichment APIs. Fair. But the hidden cost is orchestration. Running a Python process that sequentially hits 6 APIs, handles retries, manages rate limits, and writes results back to a database. That process needs a machine, uptime, monitoring, and your attention when it breaks at 2am.

Cloudflare's native MCP support in Workers changes the math. The orchestration layer moves to the edge. Tool definitions are declarative. The runtime is serverless with no cold starts at Cloudflare's scale.

I ran rough numbers on my current pipeline:

Current: ~$47/month in compute overhead for ~15,000 enrichments
Projected on Workers: ~$8/month for the same volume, with better latency

That's not the real win though. The real win is what I can build on top of it. Real-time enrichment triggered by form fills. Webhook-driven re-enrichment when data decays. Agent workflows that call enrichment tools mid-conversation without round-tripping to a central server.

The GTM infrastructure layer is moving to the edge whether we plan for it or not. MCP gives it a standard protocol.

posts.title: 61% adopted AI coding tools, 22% see results
posts.hook: 61% of engineering teams adopted AI coding assistants. Only 22% report measurable productivity gains. That gap isn't about the tools.
posts.body:
61% of engineering teams adopted AI coding assistants. Only 22% report measurable productivity gains. That gap isn't about the tools.

I use Claude Code for 6+ hours a day. It's the backbone of everything I ship. But I watched the adoption curve in my own workflow and the pattern is obvious.

Phase 1: Use it like autocomplete. Maybe 10% faster.
Phase 2: Use it for boilerplate. 20% faster on certain tasks.
Phase 3: Restructure how you work entirely. Plans, subagents, context engineering, skills files, memory systems. Different category.

Most teams are stuck in phase 1-2 and measuring "lines of code per hour" or "PR cycle time." Those metrics miss the point.

The real productivity unlock is architectural. You stop asking "can the AI write this function" and start asking "can I restructure this entire workflow so the AI handles 80% of it autonomously."

That requires rethinking how you scope work, how you write specs, how you manage context. It's a skill. And like any skill, most people plateau early because they never push past the comfortable stage.

The 22% who see results aren't using better tools. They changed how they think about work.
posts.cta: What changed your AI coding workflow from "nice to have" to "can't go back"?

inspired_by.author: Abi Noda
inspired_by.summary: New data from 400 engineering teams: 61% have adopted AI coding assistants but only 22% report a measurable productivity gain. The delta comes down to one variable — whether the team invested in prompt hygiene and context setup upfront. Tooling is table stakes. Habits are the moat.

remixes.label: adoption-curve-breakdown
remixes.hook: I've gone through four distinct phases of using AI coding tools. Most teams are stuck at phase one and calling it "adopted."
remixes.body:
I've gone through four distinct phases of using AI coding tools. Most teams are stuck at phase one and calling it "adopted."

Phase 1: Autocomplete mode. You accept tab completions. Maybe 10% faster. This is where 61% of teams live when they report "adoption."

Phase 2: Boilerplate delegation. You use it for tests, configs, repetitive code. 20% faster on specific tasks. This feels like progress but it's local optimization.

Phase 3: Architecture partner. You describe what you want at a system level. The tool generates components, you review and steer. Now you're 2-3x faster on greenfield work. This is where the 22% who see results actually live.

Phase 4: The tool has your codebase context. It reads your conventions, your memory files, your previous decisions. You're not prompting anymore. You're collaborating with something that knows your system.

I'm deep into phase 4. Claude Code reads my project files, my voice DNA, my deployment patterns. When something breaks, it checks the right database in the right workspace because the context routing is built into the system.

The gap between 61% adoption and 22% results isn't about the tool. It's about how much of your working context you've made available to the tool. Phase 1 gives it a cursor position. Phase 4 gives it your entire engineering practice.

Most teams need to stop evaluating tools and start evaluating their own context infrastructure.
remixes.cta: Which phase are you at? And what pushed you from one phase to the next?

remixes.label: contrarian-flip
remixes.hook: The 61% vs 22% AI coding stat isn't a failure of AI tools. It's a success metric for how well teams understand their own workflows.
remixes.body:
The 61% vs 22% AI coding stat isn't a failure of AI tools. It's a success metric for how well teams understand their own workflows.

Here's the uncomfortable reading of that data. The teams that see measurable gains aren't better at prompting. They already had clear coding patterns, documented conventions, and well-structured codebases before AI entered the picture.

AI coding tools amplify existing clarity. They don't create it.

I noticed this in my own setup. Claude Code became dramatically more useful the moment I invested in three things that had nothing to do with AI:

1. A CLAUDE.md file that documents every project convention, deployment target, and common mistake. This isn't for the AI. It's for me. The AI just happens to read it too.

2. A lessons file that captures every correction. When I fix a mistake, it gets logged. The next session starts by reading those lessons. Again, this is just good engineering practice that the AI leverages.

3. Context handoff documents between sessions. Not because the AI needs them. Because I need them. The AI reading them is a bonus.

Every team that reports "AI didn't help" should ask: could a new senior hire be productive in our codebase in a week? If the answer is no, the AI was never the bottleneck.

The 22% who see results didn't adopt AI. They adopted clarity. The AI just made the ROI of that clarity visible.
remixes.cta: Genuine question: did AI coding tools expose gaps in your team's documentation and conventions, or did you clean those up first?

posts.title: RevOps tech debt is the silent GTM killer
posts.hook: 40 mid-market stacks audited. Average: 14 tools with overlapping functionality and no single source of truth. I've seen this from the inside.
posts.body:
40 mid-market stacks audited. Average: 14 tools with overlapping functionality and no single source of truth. I've seen this from the inside.

When I started building GTM systems for myself, I inherited the same pattern everyone does. HubSpot for CRM, Apollo for enrichment, Outreach for sequences, Clay for transforms, 6sense for intent, Gong for calls, and a dozen Zapier automations duct-taping them together.

The annual cost? Five figures easy. The data quality? Garbage. Every tool had its own version of a contact record and none of them agreed.

So I ripped it out. Replaced most of it with SQLite, Python scripts, and API calls orchestrated by Claude Code.

Enrichment: direct API calls to providers, $0.02 per record instead of $0.15.
Scoring: a Python function, not a black-box platform.
Sequencing: Email Bison, code I control.
CRM: Attio with clean writes from one pipeline.

Total monthly cost dropped from ~$4,200 to ~$380. And the data is actually consistent because it flows through one system.

This isn't advice to go rip out your stack tomorrow. But if your RevOps team is spending more time reconciling data between tools than actually using it... the tech debt is already costing you more than the rebuild would.

remixes.label: autopsy-format
remixes.hook: I just tore apart a mid-market GTM stack. 14 tools. 23 integrations. Zero agreement on which record was the source of truth for a prospect's email.
remixes.body:
I just tore apart a mid-market GTM stack. 14 tools. 23 integrations. Zero agreement on which record was the source of truth for a prospect's email.

This isn't unusual. It's the median.

Here's what the autopsy looked like. HubSpot had the CRM record. Apollo had the enrichment data, but it was written to a custom field that nobody mapped to the standard email field. Outreach had its own contact record synced from HubSpot, except the sync broke three months ago and nobody noticed. Clay was pulling from Apollo directly, bypassing HubSpot entirely.

Four systems. Four versions of the same prospect's contact data. Three of them wrong.

The Zapier automations connecting everything? 47 active zaps. 12 broken. 8 running but producing bad data that nobody checked because the output "looked right."

This is what RevOps tech debt looks like. It's not dramatic. It's not a system going down. It's slow data decay across too many tools with too many sync points and not enough humans watching the joins.

The fix isn't fewer tools. It's an explicit data contract. One system is the source of truth for each entity. Every other system reads from it or writes to it through a defined interface. Not a Zapier automation. Not a CSV export. A contract.

I ended up rebuilding the core data flow with three tools instead of fourteen. Not because three is a magic number. Because three was enough to cover the actual workflow without creating sync ambiguity.
remixes.cta: When was the last time you audited how many versions of the same contact record exist across your stack?

remixes.label: build-vs-buy-framing
remixes.hook: Every tool in your GTM stack solved a real problem when you bought it. The tech debt isn't from bad decisions. It's from good decisions that never got reconciled.
remixes.body:
Every tool in your GTM stack solved a real problem when you bought it. The tech debt isn't from bad decisions. It's from good decisions that never got reconciled.

You bought HubSpot because you needed a CRM. Makes sense. You added Apollo because HubSpot's enrichment was weak. Fair. You added Clay because Apollo's data transforms were limited. Reasonable. You added Outreach because HubSpot sequences lacked deliverability controls. Justified.

Each decision was correct in isolation. But nobody went back to audit what the cumulative architecture looked like.

I've seen this pattern in 40 mid-market stacks now. Average: 14 tools with overlapping functionality. The overlap isn't waste. It's the result of solving problems forward without ever simplifying backward.

Here's what actually happens operationally. A prospect enters through a form. Their data touches 6 systems in the first hour. By the time a rep sees them, the record is a Frankenstein of fields populated by different tools at different times with different data freshness.

The rep doesn't know any of this. They just see a contact in their CRM and assume the data is current.

The fix isn't ripping out tools. It's establishing what I call a reconciliation layer. One place where every tool's output gets normalized, deduplicated, and timestamped before it enters the CRM. This can be a script, a database, or a purpose-built tool. The point is that it exists.

Without it, you're not running a stack. You're running 14 disconnected tools that happen to share some of the same data.
remixes.cta: If you had to pick ONE system as the source of truth for prospect data in your stack, which would it be? And does your team actually agree?

The pattern is predictable. Teams buy tools to solve immediate problems. CRM for contacts. Enrichment for data. Sequences for outreach. Intent data for targeting. Each tool is justified individually. But the cumulative architecture creates three systemic risks.

My recommendation is straightforward. Audit your current stack with one question: for each data entity (contact, company, deal), which system is the authoritative source? If the answer isn't unanimous across your team, that's your first project.

Then establish a reconciliation layer. Every tool writes to or reads from the authority through a defined interface. Not syncs. Not automations. Contracts.

Finally, consolidate where overlap is clear. In my experience, most 14-tool stacks can deliver the same functionality with 4-6 tools and dramatically better data integrity.

Teams blame the LLM when their agents fail. 9 times out of 10, the problem is what they're feeding it, not the model itself.

I run a system with skills files, memory layers, identity routing, and context handoffs between sessions. When something breaks, I almost never need a better model. I need better context.

Real examples from the last month:

→ Agent kept writing to the wrong CRM workspace. Fix: an IDENTITIES.md routing table, not a smarter prompt.

Three agent failures from last month. All three were blamed on the model. All three were context problems.

Failure 1: Agent kept writing to the wrong CRM workspace. The system had two Attio workspaces. The routing file said which one to use for which client. But the agent wasn't reading the routing file on startup. It was guessing based on the last session's context. Fix: added a mandatory identity resolution step before any CRM write. Two lines in the config.

Failure 2: Agent sent an email from the wrong account. Same root cause. Multiple Gmail accounts, no explicit routing. The agent picked the first one it found. Fix: an IDENTITIES.md file that maps every service to the correct credential. The agent reads it before any outbound action.

Failure 3: Agent recommended a tool integration that was already in the codebase. It didn't know the codebase had it because the search context was limited to the current file. Fix: expanded the context window to include the project's dependency manifest and existing integration list.

None of these needed a smarter model. GPT-4, Claude, Gemini. Wouldn't matter. The information the agent needed to make the right decision wasn't in the context when the decision happened.

This is what context engineering actually means. Not prompt engineering. Not model selection. Making sure the right information is available at the right decision point.

Most agent failures are retrieval failures wearing a model-capability mask.

remixes.label: framework-proposal
remixes.hook: I've built a four-layer context system for AI agents. It's not clever. It's boring infrastructure that prevents 90% of agent failures I used to see.
remixes.body:
I've built a four-layer context system for AI agents. It's not clever. It's boring infrastructure that prevents 90% of agent failures I used to see.

Layer 1: Identity routing. Before any action, the agent resolves which accounts, workspaces, and credentials to use. This is a flat file that maps services to identities. It prevents the "wrote to the wrong CRM" and "sent from the wrong email" class of bugs entirely.

Layer 2: Project conventions. A markdown file at the project root that describes deployment targets, naming patterns, architectural decisions, and known gotchas. The agent reads this on every session start. Think of it as onboarding docs for your AI colleague.

Layer 3: Session memory. A lessons file that captures every correction. When I fix a mistake, it gets logged with date, context, and the rule that prevents recurrence. The agent reads this file and follows every rule. Error rates drop week over week.

Layer 4: Context handoffs. At the end of every session, the agent writes a structured document describing what was done, what's pending, what broke, and what the next session needs to know. The next session reads it on startup.

None of this is sophisticated. It's file reads and a naming convention. But it turns an agent that forgets everything between sessions into one that accumulates institutional knowledge.

The total implementation is maybe 200 lines of markdown and a few config entries. The impact is the difference between an agent that works sometimes and one that works reliably.

posts.title: The signal loop is the new content strategy
posts.hook: Posting more content isn't a strategy. Owning the feedback loop between what you publish, who responds, and what you build next... that's the strategy.
posts.body:
Posting more content isn't a strategy. Owning the feedback loop between what you publish, who responds, and what you build next... that's the strategy.

I post on LinkedIn, Reddit, X, and Substack. Every platform feeds data back into the same system. A SQLite database tracks what performed, what topics resonated, which comments turned into conversations, and which conversations turned into pipeline.

Last month, a Reddit comment on r/claudedev about my enrichment workflow got 47 upvotes and 3 DMs. One of those DMs became a discovery call. The call surfaced a use case I hadn't considered. That use case became a LinkedIn post that got 2x my average engagement.

That's a signal loop. Content → response → insight → better content → pipeline.

Most teams treat content as a broadcast channel. Publish, measure impressions, repeat. The signal never flows back into product or sales.

The teams winning right now close that loop. They instrument their content the way engineers instrument their code. Every piece teaches you something. Every response is data. Every conversation is potential pipeline.

You don't need more content. You need a system that learns from the content you already publish.

Every morning, a script scans the previous day's content performance and flags patterns. Which topics got replies? Which hooks stopped the scroll? Which CTAs actually prompted people to respond versus just accumulate passive engagement?

That data feeds my content calendar. Not a guess about what to write. A signal-driven queue.

But the real loop closes when I track which conversations turned into pipeline. A Reddit comment becomes a DM. A LinkedIn reply becomes a discovery call. A Substack subscriber becomes a client.

Most people measure content by impressions or followers. That tells you reach. It doesn't tell you resonance. A post with 500 views that generates 3 qualified conversations is worth more than a post with 50,000 views and zero replies.

The system is simple. SQLite database. Python scripts on cron. A daily brief that tells me what worked and what to write next. Total infrastructure: maybe 200 lines of code.

The insight isn't the technology. It's that most content strategies are output-driven (how much can I publish?) when they should be feedback-driven (what's actually working?).

My most-liked LinkedIn post generated zero pipeline. My lowest-performing post brought in a $15k engagement. I stopped optimizing for the wrong metric.

For months, I was chasing the algorithm. Hooks that stop the scroll. Formatting tricks. Posting at optimal times. It worked. Views went up. Likes went up. Comments went up.

Revenue from content? Flat.

Then I started tracking differently. Instead of measuring engagement at the platform level, I tracked the full path. Post to comment to DM to call to deal. And the data told a completely different story.

The posts that generated business were specific, technical, and low-engagement. They spoke to a narrow audience in precise language. They got 500 views instead of 50,000. But the 12 people who read them were exactly the right people.

The viral posts attracted a broad audience that had no buying intent. The quiet posts attracted a narrow audience that was actively looking for what I build.

So I rebuilt my content system around signal, not reach. Every platform feeds data into a single database. The database tracks not just what performed on-platform, but what converted downstream. The daily brief tells me what topics generated pipeline, not what topics generated likes.

My content volume dropped by half. My pipeline from content tripled.

The math is simple. Narrow resonance beats broad reach every time if you're building a business, not a following.

posts.title: Ship log culture beats planning culture
posts.hook: I've shipped more in 6 months of weekly ship logs than I did in 2 years of quarterly planning at my last role.
posts.body:
I've shipped more in 6 months of weekly ship logs than I did in 2 years of quarterly planning at my last role.

Every week I write down what I built, what broke, and what users actually said. Not a polished update. A raw log.

This week's log:
✅ Ported the LinkedIn scout cron to pull engagement data into SQLite
✅ Built a Substack Note generator that pulls from the daily tracker
🔧 Email Bison warmup pool hit a Microsoft rate limit on 3 mailboxes
🔧 Voice drift detection flagged two posts that didn't sound like me
📊 Reddit comment pipeline: 12 scouted, 7 drafted, 4 posted, 1 DM received

None of this would show up in a quarterly OKR review. But it compounds. The scout cron feeds the content pipeline. The content pipeline feeds the signal loop. The signal loop feeds the CRM.

Planning is useful for direction. But the actual velocity comes from the discipline of shipping something small every single day and writing it down.

The log also catches drift early. If I look back at a week and it's all maintenance and no building, I know something's off before it becomes a month of stalling.

The founders and builders I respect most all have some version of this. Not a roadmap. A log.

The most productive habit I've built this year takes 12 minutes every Friday.

I open a blank doc and write three things: what I shipped, what broke, and what a real user told me. No formatting. No narrative. Just the raw record.

The magic isn't in the writing. It's in what you can't hide from.

Quarterly planning lets you bury three months of drift under a polished slide deck. A weekly ship log doesn't give you that cover. If the same task shows up three weeks in a row, you see it. If you built something nobody touched, it's right there in the log.

I started this six months ago. Since then I've ported a LinkedIn scout cron into SQLite, built a Substack generator off my daily tracker, and stood up an email warmup pipeline. None of that was on a roadmap. All of it came from staring at the log and asking: what's actually moving the needle?

The log also kills the revisionist history problem. You remember what you shipped, not what you planned to ship. That distinction matters when you're deciding what to double down on.

Planning culture rewards the deck. Ship log culture rewards the diff.

Built: what actually shipped. Not "made progress on." Shipped.
Broke: what failed, what I had to revert, what didn't land.
Heard: exact quotes from users. Not summarized feedback. Their words.

After six months of this, I can tell you the exact week my email warmup infrastructure went from flaky to stable. Quarterly reviews give you a story. Weekly logs give you data.

The uncomfortable part: you can't spin a ship log. If you didn't ship, the entry is short. That honesty compounds. You start choosing work differently when you know Friday is coming and the log doesn't lie.

posts.title: Career pivots and the plumber-to-engineer pipeline
posts.hook: I was a plumber for 10 years before I touched a CRM. The skills transferred more than you'd think.
posts.body:
I was a plumber for 10 years before I touched a CRM. The skills transferred more than you'd think.

Diagnosing why a system isn't working. Tracing the flow from input to output. Knowing that the quick patch creates a bigger problem downstream. Understanding that the customer doesn't care about your process, they care that the water runs.

That's plumbing. It's also engineering.

I see posts about career pivots that frame it as "leaving behind" the old career. I didn't leave anything behind. Every system I build now, I think about like a plumber. Where does the data flow? Where are the joints that leak? What happens when pressure spikes?

The coding agents made the pivot possible at a speed that didn't exist 3 years ago. I didn't go through a bootcamp. I didn't grind LeetCode. I learned by building things I needed, with Claude Code doing the heavy lifting on syntax while I focused on architecture and logic.

That's the part nobody talks about with AI coding tools. They don't replace thinking. They remove the barrier between thinking and building. If you already know how systems work (and a plumber absolutely does), you can build software.

The gatekeeping around "you need a CS degree" was always partly artificial. Now it's fully irrelevant.

remixes.hook: The best debugging instinct I have didn't come from a bootcamp. It came from diagnosing why a house had no water pressure.
remixes.body:
The best debugging instinct I have didn't come from a bootcamp. It came from diagnosing why a house had no water pressure.

Ten years as a plumber teaches you something that computer science courses skip: systems fail at the joints. Not in the pipes. Not in the fixtures. At the connections between them.

Software is the same. The bug is almost never in the function. It's in how the function talks to the database, how the API hands off to the frontend, how the cron job assumes the previous one finished.

Plumbing also teaches you that the customer does not care about your process. They care that the water runs. They care that it's hot when they want hot and cold when they want cold. Your elegant pipework behind the wall is invisible and irrelevant to their experience.

I carried that into every product I've built since. Nobody cares how clean your architecture is. They care that the thing works when they press the button.

The trades taught me to trace systems from input to output, to resist quick patches that create bigger problems downstream, and to respect that the end user's experience is the only metric that matters.

Tech keeps looking for talent in the same three pipelines. The most underrated engineering minds are diagnosing systems in the field right now.

The tech industry has a pipeline problem. Not the kind you think. The best systems thinkers are working in trades and we're ignoring them.

I spent a decade as a plumber before I ever opened a CRM. When people hear that, they treat it like a novelty. A fun origin story for a LinkedIn bio. But it's not a story. It's the reason I'm good at what I do.

Plumbing is diagnostics. You walk into a building where something isn't working, you trace the system from source to output, you isolate the failure point, and you fix it without breaking something else downstream. That's the job.

Tell me how that's different from debugging a production system.

The trades teach you to work under pressure with real consequences. A bad solder joint floods a basement. A skipped inspection fails a permit. There's no staging environment. Every fix is production.

They also teach you that the quick fix is usually the expensive fix. The patch that gets you out the door today creates the callback next month. Every senior engineer knows this instinct. Every tradesperson learned it with their hands.

We keep saying we want diverse backgrounds in tech. Then we filter resumes for CS degrees and bootcamp certificates. The talent is right there. We're just not looking.

posts.title: GTM engineer is the role nobody can define yet
posts.hook: "What does a GTM engineer actually do?" I get this question weekly. The answer keeps changing, which is exactly the point.
posts.body:
"What does a GTM engineer actually do?" I get this question weekly. The answer keeps changing, which is exactly the point.

Last week I:
→ Wrote a Python script that scores inbound leads against 6 enrichment signals before they hit the CRM
→ Debugged a Microsoft rate limit issue on our email warmup pool
→ Built a Reddit opportunity scanner that surfaces high-intent threads for Clearbox
→ Shipped 5 LinkedIn posts from a voice-DNA-governed content pipeline
→ Reviewed outbound copy for a client's Authority Brands campaign

That's not sales. It's not marketing. It's not engineering. It's all three, stitched together with code.

The reason CEOs don't know what this role is: it didn't exist when their org chart was designed. The GTM engineer sits in the gap between "we have tools" and "the tools actually produce revenue."

Most companies have the tools. HubSpot, Apollo, Outreach, 6sense. What they don't have is someone who can wire them together into a system that runs without manual intervention.

That's the job. Build the connective tissue between tools, data, and revenue. Automate what should be automated. Fix what's leaking.

It's plumbing for the revenue stack. And yes, I mean that literally.

posts.body:
I've built tools that nobody used. Dashboards nobody opened. Automations that solved problems nobody had. The pattern was always the same.

I built what was interesting to build instead of what someone was already trying to pay for.

Clearbox exists because I kept seeing the same Reddit threads: founders asking how to get visibility for their product, GTM teams trying to find where their buyers hang out, agencies manually scrolling subreddits for client mentions. Real people, spending real time, on a problem I could solve with a pipeline.

The failed projects? They started with "wouldn't it be cool if..." Clearbox started with "people are already doing this manually and it sucks."

The difference between a toy project and a product isn't the code quality. It's whether you found demand before you wrote the first line.

With Claude Code, I can go from idea to working prototype in a day. That speed is dangerous because it removes the natural friction that used to kill bad ideas early. You used to abandon weak ideas because they'd take weeks to build. Now you can build them in hours, launch them, watch them flatline, and wonder why.

The filter isn't "can I build this?" anymore. It's "is someone already trying to solve this with a worse tool?" If yes, build. If not, keep looking.

Every failed product I've built had the same origin story: I was excited to build it. That was the red flag.

Six micro-SaaS products. A CRM dashboard. A content scheduler. An analytics tool. A lead enrichment widget. Each one scratched my own itch to build something. None of them scratched a customer's itch to pay for something.

The pattern: I'd find a problem that was interesting to solve technically. I'd build a clean solution. I'd ship it. I'd wait for users. The users wouldn't come. Or they'd come, poke around, and leave because the problem I solved wasn't urgent enough to change their behavior.

Clearbox broke the pattern because I didn't start with an idea. I started with a signal.
